title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: When Boris and Anna Pavlovna returned to the others, Prince Hippolyte had captured the group's attention.
Leaning forward in his armchair, he said: "Le Roi de Prusse!" — and having said this, he laughed. Everyone turned toward him.

"Le Roi de Prusse?" Hippolyte repeated questioningly, laughing again, and then calmly and seriously sat back in his chair. Anna Pavlovna waited for him to continue, but as he seemed quite determined to say nothing more, she began telling how at Potsdam the godless Bonaparte had stolen the sword of Frederick the Great.

"It is the sword of Frederick the Great which I..." she began, but Hippolyte interrupted her with the words: "Le Roi de Prusse..." and again, as soon as everyone turned to look at him, excused himself and said nothing more.
Anna Pavlovna frowned. Mortemart, Hippolyte's friend, addressed him firmly.
"Come now, what about your Roi de Prusse?"
Hippolyte laughed, as if embarrassed by his own laughter.
"Oh, it's nothing. I only wanted to say..." — he had been trying all evening to work in a joke he'd heard in Vienna — "I only wanted to say that we are wrong to fight pour le Roi de Prusse!"
Boris smiled cautiously, in a way that could be taken as either ironic or appreciative, depending on how the joke landed. Everyone laughed.
"Your joke is dreadful — it's witty but unfair," said Anna Pavlovna, shaking her little shriveled finger at him.
"We are not fighting pour le Roi de Prusse, but for just principles. Oh, that wicked Prince Hippolyte!" she said.
The conversation flowed all evening, turning mainly on political news. It became particularly lively toward the end when the subject of imperial honors and awards came up.
"You know that N— N— received a snuffbox with the portrait last year?" said "the man of profound intellect." "Why shouldn't S— S— receive the same distinction?"
"I beg your pardon! A snuffbox with the Emperor's portrait is a reward, not a distinction," said the diplomat. "It's a gift, rather."
"There are precedents. I could mention Schwarzenberg."
"It's impossible," replied another.
"Will you bet? The ribbon of the order is a different matter..."
When everyone rose to leave, Helene — who had said very little all evening — turned to Boris again, asking him in a tone of caressing yet commanding significance to come to her on Tuesday.
"It's very important to me," she said, turning with a smile to Anna Pavlovna, who, with the same sad smile she wore when speaking of her exalted patroness, seconded Helene's wish.

It seemed as though something Boris had said that evening about the Prussian army had suddenly made Helene feel it was essential to see him. She seemed to promise she would explain this necessity when he came on Tuesday.

But on Tuesday evening, when Boris arrived at Helene's splendid salon, he received no clear explanation of why it had been so necessary for him to come. Other guests were there, and the countess spoke little to him. Only as he kissed her hand on leaving did she say unexpectedly, in a whisper, her face suddenly serious and unsmiling: "Come to dinner tomorrow... in the evening. You must come. Come!"
During that stay in Petersburg, Boris became a regular in the countess's household.
